structure.title: From people to political authority
structure.text: Parts I and II build an account of human motives, conflict, covenant, and the powers needed for civil peace.

structure.title: Religion and public order
structure.text: Parts III and IV examine Christian authority and rival claims to spiritual power. They continue the question of who may command.

people.name: Sovereign
people.text: The single person or assembly that everyone agrees to obey, which Hobbes argues must hold near-absolute power to keep the peace.

people.name: Covenant
people.text: The agreement by which people give up their right to do as they please and accept a common authority over them.

people.name: State of nature
people.text: Life without any government, which Hobbes famously describes as a war of everyone against everyone: solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short.

context.title: Security before trust
context.text: People may want peace yet fear that others will exploit restraint. Hobbes makes this insecurity central to the argument for political authority.
context.takeaway: Conflict need not begin with a love of violence.

context.title: Divided authority
context.text: Religious and political commands can compete for obedience. The theological sections address a practical danger to the unity Hobbes seeks.
context.takeaway: The later parts belong to the political project.

notice.why: The scope of obedience is an argument, not a simple slogan.
Hobbes builds political claims on a carefully arranged vocabulary.

opening: Two people can both want peace and still have reasons to attack first. Neither can be certain the other will keep a promise, and waiting may leave them defenceless. Hobbes builds his account of government from that predicament, amid the experience of civil war. The authority capable of ending fear must be powerful enough to make obedience safer than resistance. Following the argument means confronting how much power people might surrender for protection, and what remains of the bargain when protection fails.
